snapshot.title: UPSC History: Partition of Bengal & The Extremists
snapshot.exam_hook: 🏔️ UPSC History Hook: 1905: Partition (Curzon). Swadeshi: Boycott. Tilak: Kesari/Swaraj. 1907: Surat Split. Lal-Bal-Pal: Extremists.

quick_notes.title: Partition of Bengal (1905)
quick_notes.detail: By Lord Curzon. Reason given : Administrative convenience. Real reason : "Divide and Rule" (Dividing Hindus/Muslims). Led to the Swadeshi and Boycott Movement.
quick_notes.explanation: The Partition of Bengal was a decision made in 1905 by Lord Curzon, who was the British Viceroy of India at that time. The official reason given by the British was "administrative convenience," meaning they claimed Bengal was too large to manage as one province, but the real, hidden reason was to apply a "Divide and Rule" policy—a strategy of splitting people by religion to weaken resistance against British rule. To do this, the British divided the Bengal province into two parts: East Bengal (with a Muslim majority) and West Bengal (with a Hindu majority), setting the two communities against each other. This move provoked massive anger among Indians, who saw it as an attack on their unity, and it directly led to the Swadeshi Movement, where Indians boycotted British goods and promoted the use of Indian-made products. It also launched the Boycott Movement, which encouraged people to refuse to use British institutions, courts, and schools as a form of peaceful protest. In 1911, the British reversed the partition due to the constant protests and political pressure, reuniting Bengal, but the earlier division had already deepened religious divisions and fueled the fight for independence.

quick_notes.title: The Extremists (Lal-Bal-Pal)
quick_notes.detail: Leaders: Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, Aurobindo Ghosh. Ideology : Self-reliance, Swaraj (Self-rule), Boycott of British goods/institutions, Passive Resistance.
quick_notes.explanation: The Extremists, also known as Lal-Bal-Pal after leaders Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, and Bipin Chandra Pal (along with Aurobindo Ghosh), were a group in the Indian freedom struggle who believed in stronger, more active methods than the earlier Moderates. Their main goal was Swaraj, which means self-rule or complete independence from British control. To achieve this, they promoted self-reliance, meaning Indians should produce and use their own goods instead of depending on British imports. They called for a boycott of British goods and institutions, such as schools, courts, and councils, to harm British trade and authority. They also advocated passive resistance, which is a non-violent way of refusing to cooperate with unjust laws, like organizing protests and refusing to pay certain taxes. These ideas marked a shift from requesting reforms to demanding direct action for freedom.

quick_notes.title: Bal Gangadhar Tilak
quick_notes.detail: "Lokmanya". "Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it". Started Ganpati (1893) and Shivaji (1895) festivals to mobilize people. Journals : Kesari (Marathi), Mahratta (English).
quick_notes.explanation: Bal Gangadhar Tilak, often called Lokmanya, which means "respected by the people," was a key leader in India's freedom struggle. He famously declared, "Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it," where Swaraj means self-rule or independence from British control. To unite and inspire ordinary Indians, Tilak started two public festivals: the Ganpati festival in 1893, which celebrates the Hindu god Ganesha, and the Shivaji festival in 1895, which honors the Maratha king Shivaji. He also ran two newspapers: Kesari, written in the Marathi language, and Mahratta, written in English, to spread nationalist ideas and criticize British policies. Through these festivals and newspapers, Tilak mobilized people across different communities to join the fight for freedom.

quick_notes.title: Swadeshi Movement (1905–1908)
quick_notes.detail: Mass mobilization. Boycott of foreign cloth, picketing of shops. National education (Bengal National College). Amar Sonar Bangla (Tagore). Women and students participated for the first time.
quick_notes.explanation: The Swadeshi Movement was a mass campaign from 1905 to 1908 that urged Indians to use goods made in their own country and to stop buying British products. It began as a protest against the British government's decision to partition Bengal in 1905. The main actions included boycotting foreign cloth, which means refusing to buy or use cloth made outside India, and picketing shops that sold foreign goods, which means standing outside them to persuade customers not to enter. As part of the movement, leaders set up national education institutions like the Bengal National College, a college that taught Indian culture instead of British curriculum. The inspiring song "Amar Sonar Bangla" (meaning "My Golden Bengal") was composed by the poet Rabindranath Tagore to unite protesters. For the first time in a large political movement, women and students joined actively in marches, rallies, and picketing.

quick_notes.title: Surat Split (1907)
quick_notes.detail: INC split into Moderates and Extremists at the Surat session (Presided by Rash Behari Ghosh). Conflict over extending the Swadeshi movement outside Bengal and presidential candidates.
quick_notes.explanation: The Indian National Congress (INC), which was the main political party fighting for India's freedom from British rule, split into two groups called Moderates and Extremists during its annual meeting in Surat in 1907. The Moderates believed in using peaceful petitions and slow reforms, while the Extremists wanted more aggressive actions like boycotting British goods and demanding immediate self-rule. At this session, which was chaired by Rash Behari Ghosh as president, the two groups fought over two main issues: first, whether to spread the Swadeshi movement (a campaign urging Indians to use only Indian-made goods and reject British products) beyond the region of Bengal to the rest of India, and second, which person should be chosen as the next president of the Congress. Because they could not agree, the Extremists walked out and the Congress permanently split into two separate organizations, weakening the freedom struggle for several years.

topic_title: UPSC History: Partition of Bengal & The Extremists
lesson_intro: Today we study the 'Rise of Radicalism'. The Partition of Bengal (1905) by Lord Curzon was the spark that ignited the 'Swadeshi Movement'. It led to the rise of the 'Extremists' (Lal-Bal-Pal), who demanded 'Swaraj' as their birthright and rejected the 'Begging' methods of the Moderates. For UPSC, focus on the 'Surat Split' (1907), the concept of 'Passive Resistance', and the differences between Moderate and Extremist ideologies. This is the first mass movement of India.
